content: Carotene refers to a group of related compounds with the chemical formula C40H56. It is an orange photosynthetic pigment that plays a crucial role in photosynthesis by transferring absorbed light energy to chlorophyll. Carotene is responsible for the orange coloration of carrots and various other fruits and vegetables. Chemically, carotene is a terpene synthesized from eight isoprene units. It exists in several forms, primarily alpha-carotene (α-carotene) and beta-carotene (β-carotene), with additional forms such as gamma (γ), delta (δ), and epsilon (ε) carotene. Beta-carotene consists of two retinyl groups and is enzymatically cleaved in the small intestine by beta-carotene dioxygenase to produce retinol, a form of vitamin A. Carotene can be stored in the liver and converted to vitamin A as needed, making it a provitamin. Dietary Sources Carotene is abundant in foods such as sweet potatoes, carrots, kale, spinach, cantaloupe, turnip greens, winter squash, collard greens, cilantro, fresh thyme, romaine lettuce, goji berries, ivy gourd, cassava, and mango. The absorption of carotene from these foods is enhanced when consumed with fats, as carotene is fat-soluble. Cooking these foods for a short time until the plant cell walls break down and the color is released into any liquid also improves absorption. The Two Forms of Carotene The two primary isomers of carotene, α-carotene and β-carotene, differ in the position of double bonds in the cyclic group at the molecule's ends. Beta-carotene is the more common form and is found in yellow, orange, and green leafy fruits and vegetables, such as carrots, spinach, lettuce, tomatoes, sweet potatoes, broccoli, cantaloupe, oranges, and winter squash. Generally, the more intense the color of the fruit or vegetable, the higher its β-carotene content. While β-carotene is present in yellow-orange bell peppers, it is not the primary pigment in red bell peppers, chilies, or other Capsicum species. Plants produce a wide range of carotenoids and other colorful compounds, which serve functions such as attracting pollinators, aiding seed dispersal, and protecting cells from ultraviolet light damage. Beta-carotene is an antioxidant and helps neutralize harmful free radicals in the body. Beta-Carotene and Cancer Studies have shown that synthetic beta-carotene supplements, such as those in pill form, may increase the risk of lung and prostate cancer and overall mortality in smokers. These findings are specific to supplements and do not apply to foods naturally rich in beta-carotene. The American Cancer Society has noted that the Cancer Research Campaign has called for warning labels on beta-carotene supplements to caution smokers about the potential increased risk of lung cancer. A 1994 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine examined the relationship between daily supplementation of beta-carotene and vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) and lung cancer incidence. The study found no reduction in lung cancer rates among participants using these supplements and suggested that the supplements might have harmful effects. Similarly, a 1996 study in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute reported an increased risk of lung cancer in participants consuming beta-carotene supplements. Carotenemia Carotene is often considered beneficial due to its conversion to vitamin A in the body. However, excessive vitamin A can be harmful. Carotenemia, or hypercarotenemia, refers to an excess of carotene in the body. Unlike vitamin A toxicity, carotenemia is non-toxic but can cause yellowing of the skin, known as carotenoderma. This condition is most commonly associated with high consumption of carrots but can also indicate underlying medical conditions. A randomized trial investigating the use of β-carotene and vitamin A for lung cancer prevention was halted early due to an observed increase in lung cancer incidence among individuals with lung irritation from smoking or asbestos exposure. Production Most of the world's synthetic carotene supply is produced at a manufacturing facility in Freeport, Texas, owned by DSM. In Spain, natural beta-carotene is produced by Vitatene from the fungus Blakeslea trispora. In Australia, organic beta-carotene is derived from dried marine algae (Dunaliella salina) cultivated in harvesting ponds in Karratha, Western Australia. Carotene is also found in corn and the milk of Guernsey dairy cows, giving the milk a yellow hue. Total Synthesis Two commonly used methods for the total synthesis of β-carotene exist. The first, developed by BASF, is based on the Wittig reaction. The second, developed by Hoffmann-La Roche, is based on the Grignard reaction, building on the original synthesis by Inhoffen et al. Both methods are symmetrical, with the BASF synthesis involving a C20 + C20 approach and the Hoffmann-La Roche synthesis using a C19 + C2 + C19 approach. Nomenclature Carotenes are carotenoids that do not contain oxygen, while carotenoids with oxygen are classified as xanthophylls. The two ends of the β-carotene molecule are structurally identical and are referred to as β-rings, each consisting of nine carbon atoms. In α-carotene, one end has a β-ring, while the other end has an ε-ring. There is no such thing as an α-ring. These structural features form the basis of a systematic naming scheme: α-carotene is β,ε-carotene. β-carotene is β,β-carotene. γ-carotene, with one β-ring and one uncyclized end (ψ), is β,ψ-carotene. δ-carotene, with one ε-ring and one uncyclized end, is ε,ψ-carotene. ε-carotene is ε,ε-carotene. Six micrograms of dietary β-carotene provide the equivalent of one microgram of retinol or one Retinol Equivalent (RE), which is equal to 3⅓ International Units (IU) of vitamin A.
